tip: The l' in l'acqua is a squeezed la or il before a vowel, so it hides the gender. Acqua is feminine, shown by the -a in fredda.
In centro takes no article, where English says in THE center. Italian keeps it bare: in centro, not in il centro.
Italian keeps the article for things loved in general: amo la musica, literally 'I love the music', even though English drops the.
Giocare takes a before a sport: gioco a tennis. English 'play tennis' has no preposition, but Italian needs the a.
Alzarsi literally means 'raise yourself': ti alzi = you get up. The pronoun ti matches the subject tu.
The article, not the word ending, is the real gender signal. La pasta is feminine, so its adjective agrees: pronta, both ending in -a.
Sapere is knowing facts or how to do things: sai la risposta = you know the answer. For people or places use conoscere.
Stare covers how you are right now: non stai attento = you're not paying attention. Current states take stare, not essere.
A yes/no question keeps statement word order: puoi ripetere is 'you can repeat', turned into a question just by rising intonation.
The progressive is stare plus an -ndo form: sta cucinando = he is cooking right now.
With a reflexive, Italian uses the article, not a possessive: mi lavo i denti = I brush my teeth, literally 'the teeth'.
Opinion or doubt plus che triggers the subjunctive: credo che Maria sia partita uses sia, not è.
A modal verb attaches straight to the infinitive, no preposition: posso cambiare = I can exchange, never 'posso a cambiare'.
Al is a plus il squeezed together: al parco = a + il parco. The preposition a and the article il always merge.
The conditional can flag unconfirmed news: pioverebbe = 'supposedly it will rain', marking it as merely reported, not certain.
Sarebbe meglio plus an infinitive softens advice: sarebbe meglio partire = 'it would be better to leave', gentler than a flat command.
Lungo means 'long' as an adjective but 'along' before a noun: cammino lungo il fiume = I walk along the river.
Vicino needs a after it: abitiamo vicino al parco. English 'near the park' has no preposition, but Italian adds the a.
Italian makes routine verbs reflexive: si prepara = she prepares herself (gets ready), where English just says 'gets ready'.
An article on a time word signals a habit: la sera guardo un film = in the evenings, every evening, I watch a movie.
Ogni never changes form, and before a number it takes a plural noun: ogni cinque minuti = every five minutes.
Spending time is passare; spendere is only for money. Passiamo le vacanze = we spend the holidays.
Stare covers how you are doing: sta peggio di ieri = she is feeling worse than yesterday. Health and mood take stare.
The object pronoun can sit before the modal or attach to the infinitive: mi puoi aiutare = puoi aiutarmi, both fine.
Cos'hai is cosa + hai: cosa drops its final -a before the vowel of hai. Cos'hai fatto = what did you do.
Sto cercando = I am looking right now (stare + gerund), but Italian uses this far less than English; the plain present often covers -ing.
The progressive is optional emphasis: stai leggendo stresses that you are reading right now, but the plain leggi would also work.
Stare is for a state you are in, essere for what you are: sto attento = I am being careful; sono malato would mean I am ill.
Nascere takes essere in the past: sono nato is literally 'I am born'. The participle nato agrees with the subject.
With essere the participle agrees with the subject: sei nata ends in -a because the 'you' is female; a man would say sei nato.
Svegliarsi ends in -si, so it needs a matching pronoun: ti svegli = you wake up. The 'self' is not literal in English.
Piacere works backwards: the liked thing is the subject. Ti piace l'Italia = literally 'Italy is pleasing to you'.
Perché does double duty: it asks 'why' in a question and means 'because' in the answer. Perché sei triste = why are you sad.
Do not say io piaccio la pizza; that means 'I please the pizza'. The pizza does the pleasing: ti piace la pizza.
Use lo, not il, before a masculine noun starting with s + consonant: lo specchio. Same for z, gn, ps.
For plural liked things, piacere becomes piacciono: ti piacciono i miei quadri = the paintings please you.
C'è is 'there is', ci sono is 'there are': ci sono due camere = there are two rooms. Ci here just means 'there'.
Quantity words agree with their noun: ristoranti is masculine plural, so 'many' becomes tanti, giving tanti ristoranti.
Before an infinitive, piacere stays singular: mi piace fare colazione = I like having breakfast. The activity is the subject.
Italian has cold rather than is cold: ha freddo = she is cold. Saying sono freddo would make you a cold object.
Once the noun is plural, use ci sono, not c'è: ci sono molte persone = there are many people.
An adjective agrees with its noun: ragazza is feminine, so 'tall' becomes alta, ending in -a.
Verbs taking essere make the participle agree with the subject: siamo caduti ends in -i for 'we'.
The past uses helper verb avere plus a participle: hai chiamato = you called. Most verbs acting on an object take avere.
Imperfetto sets the background, passato prossimo marks the event: nevicava (was snowing) frames abbiamo chiuso (we closed).
Most verbs take the helper verb avere in the past: ho lavorato = I worked. Movement verbs switch to essere: sono andato.
